2. Module 5 — Lipids & Analysis
MODULE 5: FOOD LIPIDS, AUTOXIDATION AND ANALYTICAL CONSTANTS
5.1. First principle: why lipids behave differently from sugars

A sugar molecule presents many groups that interact favourably with water. A triacylglycerol presents three long hydrocarbon chains and relatively few polar groups. Water therefore does not dissolve bulk fat readily.

Uploaded-source finding: The textbook classifies lipids primarily through their hydrophobic character and solubility in organic solvents, rather than through one universal structural feature. Some lipids are amphiphilic: they contain both water-compatible and water-incompatible regions.
Functions in food and nutrition
Supply approximately nine kilocalories per gram.
Supply essential fatty acids and carry fat-soluble vitamins.
Contribute body, tenderness, texture and mouthfeel.
Carry or generate characteristic flavour compounds.
Contribute to satiety.
Participate in emulsions and biological membranes when amphiphilic.
Source: Lesson 8, pages 48–49.
5.2. Structural taxonomy
Intuitive opening

Classify a lipid by asking what appears when its major linkages are broken: only fatty acid and alcohol components, additional chemical groups, or a lipid-like constituent that is not itself a simple or compound lipid.

5.3. Fatty acid profiling
Intuitive opening
Think of a fatty acid as a carbon chain ending in a carboxyl group. Chain length affects volatility and melting; double bonds affect packing and oxidation.
The notation C18:2 means eighteen carbon atoms and two carbon–carbon double bonds. It does not, by itself, identify their positions or geometry.

Omega notation
Count from the terminal methyl end to the first double bond. Omega-3 and omega-6 describe the location of that first double bond, not the total number of double bonds.
Why polyunsaturated fatty acids are oxidation-sensitive

Hydrogen abstraction is favoured at positions that form resonance-stabilised radicals. Bis-allylic positions between double bonds are particularly vulnerable. This explains why additional unsaturation generally increases susceptibility to autoxidation under comparable conditions.
A practical comparison must still account for antioxidants, oxygen exposure, temperature, metals and the food matrix.
[HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Every unsaturated oil oxidises faster than every saturated fat under all conditions” is too absolute. Molecular susceptibility and actual storage stability are not identical.

Intuitive opening

During saponification, esterified fatty acids are converted into soaps. A small collection of lipid-associated substances does not become fatty acid soap and can be recovered as the unsaponifiable fraction.

blocks.text: Sterol acetate melting-point test
Principle: Convert isolated sterols into their acetates and examine their melting behaviour. A higher-melting phytosterol-containing fraction can indicate vegetable-fat addition to an animal fat.
Limitations: Mixtures, purification, recrystallisation and the fat’s natural composition affect interpretation. This is not an infallible standalone identification of every adulterant.

Squalene has thirty carbon atoms, not forty.
The textbook reports squalene at approximately one to seven grams per kilogram in olive oil and approximately 3.3 grams per kilogram in rice oil.

5.6. Autoxidation: the free-radical chain reaction
Intuitive opening

A radical is a species containing an unpaired electron. Once a lipid radical reacts with oxygen, the resulting peroxyl radical can remove hydrogen from another lipid molecule. One initiation event can therefore sustain many propagation steps.
Let RH represent an oxidisable lipid and R• its carbon-centred radical.

INITIATION
RH + initiating radical --> R• + hydrogenated initiator

PROPAGATION
R• + O2 --> ROO•
ROO• + RH --> ROOH + R•

TERMINATION
R• + R• --> nonradical product
R• + ROO• --> nonradical product
ROO• + ROO• --> nonradical products

SECONDARY DECOMPOSITION
ROOH --> reactive intermediates --> aldehydes, ketones,
                                  alcohols, acids and hydrocarbons
Stepwise interpretation
Initiation: Heat, light-related processes or metal-catalysed reactions help generate radicals or decompose pre-existing hydroperoxides.
Propagation: The lipid radical adds oxygen. The peroxyl radical generates a hydroperoxide and another lipid radical.
Termination: Two radicals react, removing chain carriers.
Hydroperoxide decomposition: Primary oxidation products break down into secondary products, many of which produce objectionable odours.
Hydroperoxides are generally not the principal volatile rancid-odour compounds. Their decomposition products are central to rancid flavour.
Important controls

rows: Limit headspace oxygen and oxygen entry
Avoid contamination and unsuitable contact surfaces
Alters catalysts, mobility and interfacial behaviour
Do not assume that drying always prevents oxidation

Lipid peroxyl radical + antioxidant hydrogen donor

                      v
Lipid hydroperoxide + relatively stabilised antioxidant radical
Chemical clarification: Photooxidation, especially singlet-oxygen oxidation, is not identical to the ordinary free-radical autoxidation sequence.
[HPSC EXAM TRAP] A low peroxide value can describe fresh oil or extensively heated oil whose hydroperoxides have decomposed. Interpret it with processing history and other measurements.
5.7. Hydrolytic and ketonic rancidity
Hydrolytic rancidity
Water breaks ester linkages; lipases accelerate the reaction in suitable conditions.

Triacylglycerol + water --> diacylglycerol + free fatty acid
Diacylglycerol + water --> monoacylglycerol + free fatty acid
Monoacylglycerol + water --> glycerol + free fatty acid
The complete net hydrolysis consumes three water molecules per triacylglycerol.
Consequences:
Increased acidity and acid value.
Objectionable flavour when sufficient short-chain fatty acids are released.
Reduced smoke point in frying oil.
Desirable flavour development when carefully controlled during certain cheese-ripening processes.
At deep-frying temperatures, substantial hydrolysis does not require survival of the original food lipase; heat and food-derived water are sufficient contributors.
Ketonic rancidity
Source gap: Ketonic rancidity is not developed in the supplied textbook sections. The following is a chemical clarification of the requested term, not an attributed textbook passage.
Certain fungi can convert fatty acids through incomplete beta-oxidative pathways into beta-keto acids. Decarboxylation produces methyl ketones.
Fatty acid --> beta-keto acid --> methyl ketone + carbon dioxide
A beta-keto acid can be represented as:
R-CO-CH2-COOH --> R-CO-CH3 + CO2
Medium-chain substrates are important. Related methyl-ketone formation can be desirable in blue-cheese flavour, while uncontrolled formation elsewhere is a defect.

Acid value or free fatty acid measurement
No; controlled lipolysis can develop cheese flavour

Intuitive opening

Milligrams of potassium hydroxide per gram
How much halogen-equivalent uptake reflects unsaturation?
Grams of iodine per one hundred grams of fat

Milliequivalents of active oxygen per kilogram

blocks.text: A. Saponification value
Definition: Milligrams of potassium hydroxide required to saponify one gram of fat under the prescribed conditions.
Principle: Reflux the fat with a known excess of alcoholic potassium hydroxide. Back-titrate unused alkali with standard acid. A reagent blank measures the initial alkali available.
Triacylglycerol + 3 KOH --> glycerol + 3 potassium fatty acid salts
$$Saponification\ value = \frac{56.1(B-S)N}{m}$$
Where:
B is the blank acid titre in millilitres.
S is the sample acid titre in millilitres.
N is the acid normality.
m is sample mass in grams.
56.1 is the relevant potassium hydroxide mass-conversion factor.
For an ideal pure triacylglycerol:
$$Saponification\ value \approx \frac{168300}{M}$$
Here M is its molar mass in grams per mole. Three ester bonds account for the factor of three.
Interpretation: Shorter average fatty acid chains generally mean more triacylglycerol molecules per gram and therefore a higher saponification value.
Qualification: Free fatty acids, unsaponifiable matter and degradation products affect the relationship. It is not a direct chain-length ruler for every degraded or mixed sample.
Hypothetical worked example: Blank titre 25.0 millilitres; sample titre 10.0 millilitres; acid normality 0.5; fat mass 2.0 grams.
Report approximately 210.4 milligrams of potassium hydroxide per gram.
B. Iodine value
Definition: Grams of iodine absorbed, expressed as iodine equivalent, by one hundred grams of fat under the prescribed method.
Principle: Halogen reagent reacts with carbon–carbon double bonds. The unreacted reagent is determined iodometrically.
$$Iodine\ value = \frac{12.69(B-S)N}{m}$$
Here the titres are thiosulphate titres in millilitres, N is thiosulphate normality and m is sample mass in grams.
Interpretation: Greater double-bond content per unit mass generally gives a higher iodine value. The fatty acid chain length and sample composition also influence the result.
Frying connection: Oxidative and polymerisation reactions consume or alter unsaturation, so iodine value commonly decreases.
[HPSC EXAM TRAP] Iodine value measures a bulk unsaturation-related property; it does not identify the omega family or distinguish every cis and trans isomer.
C. Peroxide value
Definition: A primary oxidation index conventionally expressed as milliequivalents of active oxygen per kilogram of fat.
Principle: Peroxide-related oxidants liberate iodine from iodide under the method conditions. Titrate the liberated iodine with sodium thiosulphate.

ROOH + 2 I- + 2 H+ --> ROH + I2 + H2O
I2 + 2 thiosulphate ions --> 2 I- + tetrathionate ion
$$Peroxide\ value = \frac{1000(S-B)N}{m}$$
Where sample and blank titres are in millilitres and sample mass is in grams.
Hypothetical worked example: Sample titre 1.50 millilitres; blank titre 0.10 millilitre; thiosulphate normality 0.01; sample mass 5.0 grams.
Result: 2.8 milliequivalents per kilogram.
Limitation: Formation and destruction occur simultaneously. A decreasing peroxide value during heating does not prove restoration of quality.
D. Reichert–Meissl value
Definition: Millilitres of 0.1 normal alkali needed to neutralise the steam-volatile, water-soluble fatty acids obtained from five grams of fat under the prescribed procedure.
Principle: Saponify, acidify to release fatty acids, distil under specified conditions, separate the appropriate soluble fraction and titrate it.
Principal teaching association: Butyric and caproic acids; useful in examination discussions of butter and ghee identity and purity.
For a complete recovered fraction:
$$Value = (S-B)\frac{N}{0.1}$$

If only an aliquot is titrated, multiply by the prescribed total-volume-to-aliquot factor. In a method using a 100-millilitre aliquot from 110 millilitres, that factor is 1.1. Do not insert this factor into every method indiscriminately.
Qualification: This is an operationally defined distillation value, not an exhaustive measurement of every water-soluble fatty acid in the original fat.
E. Polenske value
Definition: Millilitres of 0.1 normal alkali needed to neutralise the steam-volatile, water-insoluble fatty acids obtained from five grams of fat under the prescribed procedure.
Principle: Recover the insoluble volatile acid fraction, dissolve it in the specified solvent and titrate.
Principal teaching association: Caprylic and capric acids, with contributions depending on the method; useful for recognising lauric-fat addition.
For the complete recovered fraction:
$$Value = (S-B)\frac{N}{0.1}$$
Important distinction: Coconut and palm-kernel fats are the relevant lauric-fat comparison. Plain palm oil should not be substituted for palm-kernel oil in a mechanistic explanation.
F. Acid value: the essential companion measurement
Definition: Milligrams of potassium hydroxide required to neutralise the free acids in one gram of sample.
$$Acid\ value = \frac{56.1(S-B)N}{m}$$
Unlike saponification value, acid value does not deliberately count the alkali required to hydrolyse all ester bonds.
If free fatty acids are reported as oleic acid:
$$Free\ fatty\ acids\ (percent) = \frac{28.25(S-B)N}{m}$$
Approximately:
$$Free\ fatty\ acids\ as\ oleic\ acid\ (percent) = \frac{Acid\ value}{1.99}$$
The conversion changes when a different reference fatty acid is used.

3. Deep-Frying Dynamics
DEEP-FAT FRYING: TRANSPORT, REACTION AND QUALITY CONTROL
Core source: Food Chemistry, Lesson 9, printed pages 53–55.
1. First principle: frying is not merely heating food in oil

A fryer is simultaneously a heat-transfer system, a water-removal system and a chemically reactive lipid environment. Food introduces moisture and solids; the oil supplies heat and becomes part of the finished product.
The textbook describes frying at approximately 180 degrees Celsius. This is a representative operating temperature, not a legal requirement that every food must be fried at exactly that temperature.
2. Physical events at the food–oil interface

Food enters hot oil
        |
        +--> Heat enters the food
        |
        +--> Water moves outward and becomes steam
        |         |
        |         +--> Agitation of oil
        |         +--> Steam stripping of volatile compounds
        |         +--> Water available for hydrolysis
        |
        +--> Crust and pore structure develop
        |
        +--> Oil is carried with or absorbed into the product
        |
        +--> Food lipids and solids may enter the frying medium
Steam distillation of volatiles
Water released by food sweeps some volatile oxidation products out of the oil. Their concentration may approach a plateau when formation is balanced by evaporation, stripping or further reaction.
Critical inference: Removal of volatile compounds does not remove the entire nonvolatile degradation burden.
Steam blanket
The textbook notes that steam above the oil can reduce oxygen availability at the surface. This protective tendency does not eliminate oxidation throughout the fryer.
Fat uptake
Uploaded-source finding: Finished fried foods may contain approximately 5–40% fat by mass; potato chips are illustrated at approximately 35%.
These are broad product examples. They are not a universal absorption fraction for every food, nor are they a legal maximum.
Chemical interpretation: Product porosity, surface condition, drainage and cooling affect retained oil. The amount measured includes more than one possible uptake mechanism.
Lipid exchange
Chicken and other fatty foods can release endogenous lipids into the oil. The resulting frying medium may have a different fatty acid composition and oxidative stability from the starting oil.

blocks.text: 4. Thermal oxidation
Intuitive opening
At room temperature, hydroperoxides may accumulate long enough to be measured. At frying temperature, they can decompose rapidly. The balance shifts toward secondary and nonvolatile products.

Unsaturated lipid + oxygen

            v
Hydroperoxides and related intermediates
            |
            +--> Cleavage --> volatile aldehydes, ketones, acids and alcohols
            |
            +--> Oxygenated nonvolatile compounds
            |
            +--> Radical formation --> coupled and polymerised products
Product classes identified by the textbook
Volatile compounds: saturated and unsaturated aldehydes, ketones, hydrocarbons, lactones, alcohols, acids and esters.
Nonpolymeric polar compounds: examples include hydroxyl and epoxy acids.
Dimeric and polymeric acids and glycerides.

Peroxide-value paradox
The textbook explicitly describes peroxide content increasing after an induction period and subsequently decreasing.
[HPSC EXAM TRAP] “The peroxide value of repeatedly heated oil must increase continuously” is incorrect. Hydroperoxide decomposition can outpace formation.

Food continually supplies water. Cleavage of ester bonds releases free fatty acids and partial glycerides.
Uploaded-source finding: Liberation of free fatty acids causes a decrease in smoke point.
Chemical clarification: Smoke point also depends on the oil’s refining history and other components. A free-fatty-acid concentration is not the sole universal determinant.

More water exposure + thermal history

More ester cleavage and free fatty acids

6. Polymerisation
Intuitive opening
When reactive lipid chains join, the average molecular size rises. Large molecules move less easily, so viscosity increases.
The textbook describes cyclic and noncyclic products involving carbon–carbon linkages and oxygen bonding.

Darker oil.

blocks.text: Reconciling polymerisation with saponification-value changes

Polymerisation alone increases molecular size and can suggest a lower alkali demand per unit mass. Frying, however, produces a mixture that also includes cleavage products and free acids. The net measured direction reflects competing processes. This is why the ideal pure-triacylglycerol equation must not be applied mechanically to degraded frying oil.

10. Total Polar Compounds: interpretation and statutory boundary
What the measurement means

Chemical clarification: Total Polar Compounds represent a broad method-defined group of polar constituents in oil. These can include oxidised lipids, partial glycerides, free fatty acids and some degradation-related products. It is not another name for peroxide value and does not represent one single toxic chemical.
A compositional expression is:
$$Total\ polar\ compounds\ (percent) = \frac{Mass\ of\ polar\ fraction}{Mass\ of\ oil\ sample}\times100$$
Reference fractionation and rapid instrumental estimates are not automatically interchangeable without calibration and validation.

11. Defensible quality-control approach
Control time and temperature rather than relying only on appearance.

6.1. First principle: an enzyme changes reaction speed, not the equilibrium destination

An enzyme provides a lower-energy route to a chemical transformation. It does not supply unlimited energy, make an unfavourable process favourable by itself, or alter the equilibrium constant of the uncoupled reaction.
The textbook treats enzymes as proteinaceous biological catalysts with an active centre. The active site includes regions important for substrate binding and catalysis.

Intuitive opening

An inhibitor may prevent substrate binding, disable catalytic turnover after binding, or bind preferentially to the enzyme–substrate complex. The kinetic effect depends on which enzyme forms it binds and how strongly.

Let:
$$\alpha = 1+\frac{[I]}{K_i}$$
$$\alpha' = 1+\frac{[I]}{K_i'}$$
Here I is inhibitor concentration, Ki describes binding to free enzyme, and Ki′ describes binding to the enzyme–substrate complex.
Then:
$$v_0 = \frac{V_{max}[S]}{\alpha K_m+\alpha'[S]}$$
Consequently:
$$V_{max,app} = \frac{V_{max}}{\alpha'}$$

Competitive inhibition
For competitive inhibition, alpha-prime equals one.
Apparent Michaelis constant increases by the factor alpha.
Maximum rate stays unchanged.
Reciprocal-plot lines share the vertical intercept.
Slope increases.

Maximum rate decreases.
Michaelis constant remains unchanged.
Reciprocal-plot lines share the horizontal intercept.
Vertical intercept and slope increase.
Binding away from the substrate-binding site is not enough, by itself, to prove these exact kinetic changes.

For uncompetitive inhibition, alpha equals one and alpha-prime exceeds one.
Maximum rate decreases.
Michaelis constant decreases by the same factor.
Their ratio, and therefore reciprocal-plot slope, remains unchanged.
Reciprocal-plot lines are parallel.
A lower apparent Michaelis constant does not mean the inhibited enzyme processes substrate more successfully; the maximum rate is also lower.

8.3. Definitions under Regulation 2
Fortification
Deliberately increasing the content of essential micronutrients in food to improve its nutritional quality and provide a public-health benefit with minimal risk to health.
Fortificant
A substance added to food to provide micronutrients; the definition excludes nutraceuticals and foods for Special Dietary Uses.
Fortified food
A food specified under the Food Safety and Standards (Food Products Standards and Food Additives) Regulations, 2011, that has undergone fortification according to these regulations.
Fortified Processed Foods

Processed foods altered from their natural state by industrial processing methods and fortified according to these regulations. They may use fortified staples as raw materials and/or be fortified with permitted micronutrients and additives under the referenced food-products and additives framework.
Micronutrients
Essential dietary nutrients, including vitamins, minerals and trace elements, required in very small quantities and important for development, disease prevention and well-being.
Staple foods
Foods intended for mass consumption on a daily basis, including rice, wheat, wheat flour, atta, maida, oil, salt, milk and other foods designated under the regulations.
Government-funded programme
A programme, policy, scheme or other provision through which Central or State Governments sell, distribute or otherwise make food available to the public.
Quality assurance
Systematic measures taken by manufacturers and packers throughout manufacturing or packing to ensure that the finished food complies with the Act and applicable standards and regulations.

blocks.text: Complete model answer
Introduction

Deep-fat frying exposes edible oil to high temperature, commonly around 180 degrees Celsius in the uploaded textbook, while food continuously supplies water, solids and sometimes endogenous lipids. Repeated heating and cooling therefore produce a changing reaction mixture rather than merely warming an unchanged oil. Hydrolysis, thermal oxidation and polymerisation progressively alter physical behaviour, composition and analytical indices.
1. Physical alterations

Moisture release and steam stripping: Water leaving the food becomes steam, agitates the oil and strips some volatile degradation products. Consequently, volatile-product concentrations may approach a plateau even while nonvolatile degradation continues. A steam blanket may reduce oxygen availability above the surface, but it does not eliminate oxidation.

Oil uptake and lipid exchange: The textbook reports approximately 5–40% fat by mass in finished fried foods, with potato chips illustrated at approximately 35%. These are product-dependent examples, not universal absorption limits. Fat released from foods such as chicken can change the composition and oxidative stability of the frying medium.
Increasing viscosity: Coupled and polymerised lipid products increase molecular size and viscosity. Oil may drain less effectively and the product may become greasy.

Foaming, darkening and deposits: Polar degradation products and accumulated food material contribute to persistent foaming, darkening, gums and residues. Normal steam bubbling during frying must be distinguished from deterioration-associated persistent foam.

Reduced smoke point: Accumulation of free fatty acids contributes to smoking at lower temperatures. Smoke point is nevertheless influenced by other oil constituents and cannot alone establish compliance.
2. Chemical alterations
A. Hydrolysis
Food-derived water promotes cleavage of triacylglycerol ester bonds under frying conditions:

Triacylglycerol + water --> diacylglycerol + free fatty acid
Diacylglycerol + water --> monoacylglycerol + free fatty acid
Monoacylglycerol + water --> glycerol + free fatty acid

Complete hydrolysis consumes three water molecules per triacylglycerol. The resulting free fatty acids increase acidity and contribute to a lower smoke point. This high-temperature hydrolysis does not require the original food lipase to remain active.
B. Thermal oxidation
Unsaturated lipid chains undergo oxygen-associated oxidation. A simplified chain mechanism is:

Lipid radical + oxygen --> lipid peroxyl radical
Lipid peroxyl radical + lipid --> hydroperoxide + new lipid radical
Hydroperoxide --> reactive intermediates --> secondary products

Hydroperoxide decomposition generates aldehydes, ketones, alcohols, acids and hydrocarbons. Volatile products contribute to flavour changes and may partly escape with steam. Oxygenated nonvolatile compounds remain in the oil. Temperature, oxygen exposure, metals, oil composition and heating duration govern the extent of deterioration.
C. Polymerisation and thermal alteration

Reactive lipid chains combine through carbon–carbon and oxygen-containing linkages. Cyclic monomers, dimers, trimers and higher polymers can form. Their accumulation increases viscosity, foaming, gum deposition and potentially oil retention by food. The textbook associates greater unsaturation and longer frying time with increased polymerisation under comparable conditions.

4. Why peroxide value alone is inadequate
Peroxide value measures peroxide-related primary oxidation, conventionally expressed as milliequivalents of active oxygen per kilogram. It does not measure cumulative deterioration.
The central kinetic distinction is:
$$\frac{d[Hydroperoxides]}{dt}=Formation\ rate-Decomposition\ rate$$

If decomposition exceeds formation, hydroperoxide concentration falls despite continuing deterioration. High frying temperatures favour rapid decomposition, and the textbook explicitly describes peroxide content rising and later falling.
Peroxide value alone is therefore inadequate for five reasons:
Hydroperoxides are unstable at frying temperatures. A small measured pool may reflect rapid destruction rather than little oxidation.
Secondary oxidation products are not comprehensively measured. Aldehydes, ketones and other products may accumulate after hydroperoxides disappear.
Hydrolysis is a different deterioration pathway. Free fatty acids can increase without a corresponding peroxide-value increase.
Polymerisation is not represented adequately. High-molecular-mass deterioration products can persist when peroxide value is low.
Thermal and sampling history matter. Cooling and oxygen exposure can alter the measured primary-oxidation pool. Oils with different histories cannot be ranked reliably by this index alone.

Fresh oil ------------------------------> low peroxide value
Severely heated oil with decomposition -> potentially low peroxide value

Same index range does not imply the same quality history.
5. Integrated assessment and control

Used frying oil should be assessed through a combination of processing history, acidity, appropriate primary- and secondary-oxidation measures, polar-product or polymer assessment, and physical observations. Good practice includes controlling temperature, avoiding prolonged idle heating, managing food debris and preventing uncontrolled repeated thermal cycling.

Continuous replenishment can limit accumulation under some operating conditions, as explained by the textbook, but adding fresh oil does not prove that the resulting mixture is compliant or justify indefinite use.
Conclusion

Repeated frying produces interconnected hydrolytic, oxidative and polymerisation changes. Peroxide value is useful for primary oxidation, but its rise-and-fall behaviour makes it unreliable as a standalone used-oil quality test. A defensible decision combines complementary analytical measures with the verified applicable regulatory criterion.
Worked analytical illustration
This is a hypothetical calculation, not measured data from the uploads.
For iodometric peroxide-value measurement:
$$Peroxide\ value=\frac{1000(V_s-V_b)N_t}{m}$$
Where:
Vs is sample sodium-thiosulphate titre in millilitres.
Vb is blank titre in millilitres.
Nt is sodium-thiosulphate normality.
m is oil sample mass in grams.
Assume sample titre 1.50 millilitres, blank titre 0.10 millilitre, normality 0.01 and sample mass 5.00 grams.
$$Peroxide\ value=14\div5.00=2.8\ milliequivalents\ per\ kilogram$$
Permissible inference: The assay detects the stated peroxide-related oxidation level under its conditions.
Impermissible inference: The oil must be fresh, safe or legally suitable for further frying. Those conclusions require additional evidence.
Legal caveat: Total Polar Compounds thresholds

The requested revision targets are 15% for fresh oil and 25% for used frying oil. Neither uploaded document establishes their governing legal provision or exact boundary wording. Accordingly, this source-limited model does not represent them as verified statutory limits.

Before quoting these figures as law, verify the relevant food-products standard or notification, its current amendment status, the relevant oil category, the method and the exact discard rule. “Not more than 25%” and “25% or more shall not be used” have different consequences at exactly 25%. Do not silently equate them.
[HPSC EXAM TRAP] “Low peroxide value proves that a used frying oil is suitable for reuse” is scientifically invalid even before the legal criterion is considered.

blocks.text: Complete model answer
Introduction

The Food Safety and Standards (Fortification of Foods) Regulations, 2018 establish a food-vehicle-specific framework for deliberately increasing essential micronutrients to improve nutritional quality and provide public-health benefit with minimal health risk. The uploaded 30 September 2021 compendium connects nutrient standards with permitted sources, packaging, labelling, quality assurance and generally applicable food law.
Fortification is therefore not simply a nutrient-addition claim: it is a regulated process requiring suitable composition, reliable manufacturing control and appropriate consumer information.
1. Definitions and statutory scope
Under Regulation 2:
Fortification means deliberately increasing the content of essential micronutrients in a food to improve its nutritional quality and provide public-health benefit with minimal health risk.
Fortificant means a substance added to food to provide micronutrients; the definition excludes nutraceuticals and foods for Special Dietary Uses.
Fortified food is a food specified under the Food Products Standards and Food Additives Regulations, 2011 that has undergone fortification in accordance with these regulations.
Micronutrients include essential dietary vitamins, minerals and trace elements needed in very small quantities and important to development, disease prevention and wellbeing.
Staple foods are articles intended for daily mass consumption, including rice, wheat, wheat flour, atta, maida, oil, salt, milk and other designated staples.
Quality assurance means systematic measures throughout manufacturing or packing to ensure compliance of the finished fortified food.

The regulations state that they supersede earlier fortification standards under the Act, while preserving the specified exception concerning regulations on nutraceuticals and foods for Special Dietary Uses.
2. General principles under Regulation 3

Micronutrient addition may contribute to preventing or correcting demonstrated deficiency, improving inadequate nutritional status, meeting recommended intake, maintaining or improving health, and maintaining or improving nutritional quality.

Mandatory fortification must be grounded in the severity and extent of public-health need, demonstrated by generally accepted scientific evidence. The Food Authority may specify mandatory fortification of a staple on direction of the Government of India. Hence, “when fortified, shall” is not equivalent to universal compulsory fortification of every product.
Where iron is used as a nutrient source, heme iron shall not be used in any form in any article of food under Regulation 3(4).

For fortified processed foods, Regulations 3(5)–3(7) provide for preparation using fortified food articles that may be cereals or milk, a 15–30% Indian adult recommended-dietary-allowance framework based on 600 kilocalories from processed foods, and exclusion of High Fat Sugar Salt foods from that category.
3. Schedule I standards for fortified staples
A. Iodized salt and double fortified salt

rows: Iodine in iodized salt and double fortified salt, using the August 2021 substituted provision
15–30 parts per million on a dry-weight basis

blocks.text: The earlier displayed iodine provision distinguished 20–30 parts per million at manufacture and 15–30 at distribution, including retail. The August 2021 amendment substitutes the single 15–30 parts-per-million dry-weight range. The compendium states commencement of that amendment on 27 August 2021 and compliance by 1 March 2022.
The salt footnotes also matter:
Where an anticaking agent is added, total water-insoluble matter shall not exceed 2.2%.
Sodium chloride content in the applicable iodized-salt footnote shall not be less than 97% by weight on a dry basis; other referenced salt parameters also apply.
Double fortified salt may contain food-grade hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose, titanium dioxide, fully hydrogenated soybean oil and sodium hexametaphosphate.
The double-fortified-salt footnote permits an anticaking agent not exceeding 2% on a dry-weight basis and specifies the 2.2% water-insoluble-matter ceiling where such an agent is used.
The express double-fortified-salt provision is why a general textbook statement about inorganic colouring matter must not be misread as prohibiting every inorganic additive in every food.
B. Fortified vegetable oil

rows: Cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol, only from plant source

blocks.text: Both listed vitamins are specified when vegetable oil is fortified under this category. The plant-source qualification concerns vitamin D; it does not mean that only vitamin D2 can qualify.
C. Fortified milk

The category includes species-identified buffalo, cow, goat, sheep and camel milk, as well as full cream, toned, double toned, skimmed and standardized milk. The milk is to undergo pasteurization, sterilization, ultra-high-temperature sterilization or treatment, or boiling.

rows: Cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol, only from plant source

blocks.text: These are per-litre milk standards, not per-gram oil standards.
D. Fortified atta and maida
Both vehicles require added iron, folic acid and vitamin B12 when fortified under their respective Schedule I provisions.

rows: Ferrous citrate, ferrous lactate, ferrous sulphate, ferric pyrophosphate, electrolytic iron, ferrous fumarate or ferrous bisglycinate
Sodium iron (III) ethylene diamine tetra acetate trihydrate, also described as sodium feredetate

blocks.text: The schedule explains the higher level of the first iron alternative as accounting for lower bioavailability.
Multigrain atta may use the fortified-atta levels provided it contains more than 50% wheat flour. Exactly 50% does not satisfy the literal “more than” condition.
E. Fortified rice

rows: Sodium iron (III) ethylene diamine tetra acetate trihydrate, also described as sodium feredetate

blocks.text: Rice and flour share the principal nutrient ranges, but not the complete iron-source list. The August 2021 amendment replaces the heading “Fortified Raw Rice” with “Fortified Rice”.
F. Optional additions to atta, maida and rice
These may be added singly or in combination. Optional status does not make their specified source and level irrelevant when an addition is made.
G. Fortified milk powder

The August 2021 insertion requires vitamin A and vitamin D levels that yield compliant fortified milk after reconstitution according to the label. The powder is restricted to Government-funded programmes for preparing reconstituted fortified milk.
Its label must additionally state that:
It is not recommended for direct consumption.
It is only for use under the named Government-funded programme.
It is to be consumed only after reconstitution of the entire contents according to the label directions.
Once opened, the pack is to be consumed on the same day.
The compendium states that this amendment was in force from 27 August 2021, with compliance by 1 March 2022.
4. Packaging, declaration, logo and mandatory iron advisory
Packaging

Regulation 7(1) requires packaging to consider the nature of the added fortificant and its effect on shelf life. Appropriate packaging must therefore protect nutrient retention and the food’s quality; merely adding a nutrient at manufacture does not remove storage-related obligations.
Fortification declaration and logo
Regulation 7(2) requires the package to carry the words “fortified with” followed by the name of the fortificant, together with the prescribed Schedule II logo.
The same provision says the package may also carry the tagline “Sampoorna Poshan Swasth Jeevan” under the logo. The tagline is optional under this wording.

Express exception: The requirements of Regulation 7(2) do not apply to iodized salt when fortified with iodine. This does not exempt that salt from every other labelling requirement, nor does it automatically exempt iron-containing double fortified salt.
The accessible Schedule II extraction does not establish numerical graphic dimensions or a Pantone specification. These must not be invented or attributed to the uploaded text.
Iron-fortified food advisory
The substituted Regulation 7(4) requires every package of iron-fortified food to carry:
People with Thalassemia may take under medical supervision and persons with Sickle Cell Anaemia are advised not to consume iron fortified food products.

This wording distinguishes medical supervision for people with thalassemia from the non-consumption advice for persons with sickle cell anaemia. Do not replace the two-part advisory with the earlier thalassemia-only statement.
The compendium states that this amendment was in force from 27 August 2021, with compliance by 1 March 2022.

Regulation 7 also applies the general packaging and labelling provisions named in the compendium and permits compliant manufacturers and packers to make nutrition claims under the referenced framework. This is not authorization for unsupported therapeutic or disease-cure claims.
5. Quality assurance obligations under Regulation 5

Every manufacturer and packer must give an undertaking on quality assurance and submit evidence to the Food Authority or its designated authority. The undertaking is required twice a year and must include:
Notified-laboratory certification: Certification by a food laboratory notified by the Food Authority that the fortified food complies with the Act, regulations and standards.
Records and inventory: Up-to-date records and continuous inventory of fortificants, including their procurement sources.
Stage-wise monitoring: Appropriate monitoring procedures at different manufacturing or packing stages.
Random testing: Testing of fortificants and fortified food.
Equipment and process audit: Regular audit of technical equipment and processes.
Good manufacturing practices: Application of practices specified by the Food Authority from time to time.

Purity criteria: The provision allows adoption of generally accepted micronutrient purity criteria associated with the Indian Pharmacopoeia, British Pharmacopoeia, Food Chemical Codex, Joint Food and Agriculture Organization or World Health Organization Expert Committee on Food Additives, or Codex Alimentarius.
The permissive wording concerning adoption of referenced purity criteria should not be transformed into a requirement to use all listed references simultaneously.

Regulation 6 requires generally applicable compliance for both voluntarily and mandatorily fortified food. Manufacturing, packing, labelling, handling, distribution and sale remain subject to the Act and regulations, whether undertaken for profit or through a Government-funded programme.
6. Label range and analytical tolerance

The September 2021 substitution of Regulation 4(1) requires the added micronutrients declared on the label to fall within Schedule I ranges. It allows a tolerance of minus 10% of the declared total value on the label for compliance and analysis at any point in time, while expressly requiring compliance with the Schedule I maximum for added micronutrients.
The compendium states that this amendment was in force from 22 September 2021, with compliance by 1 April 2022.
Three distinctions follow:
Declared added micronutrient levels must be within the applicable prescribed range.
A negative analytical tolerance is not an authorization for a ten-percent upward excess.
“Added micronutrients” and “declared total value” are different phrases in the provision and must not be silently treated as identical where intrinsic nutrients contribute.
7. Critical evaluation

The framework combines public-health purpose with product-specific limits and consumer safeguards. Permitted-source restrictions address more than nutrient quantity: bioavailability, food compatibility and stability affect the suitability of the fortificant. The different iron-source ranges illustrate the importance of chemical form.

Effective implementation nevertheless depends on manufacturing uniformity, appropriate mixing, representative sampling, nutrient retention, label accuracy and documented quality assurance. A compliant-looking logo is not a substitute for actual nutrient content or reliable process control.

Fortified processed foods require separate Schedule III assessment, and High Fat Sugar Salt exclusion prevents nutrient addition from automatically converting a disqualified processed food into an eligible fortified processed product.
Conclusion

Fortification under the uploaded FSSAI framework is a coordinated system of public-health justification, vehicle-specific nutrient standards, permitted sources, packaging and labelling safeguards, and documented quality assurance. Strong compliance requires both accurate nutrient addition and continued verification of the food placed on the market.
Worked statutory calculations
Calculation 1 — Parts per million in double fortified salt
For mass concentration:
$$1\ part\ per\ million=1\ milligram\ per\ kilogram$$
Therefore, the prescribed iron range of 850–1100 parts per million as iron corresponds to:
$$850–1100\ milligrams\ of\ iron\ per\ kilogram\ of\ salt$$
For a hypothetical 100-kilogram quantity assessed on the applicable mass basis:
$$850\times100=85000\ milligrams=85\ grams$$
$$1100\times100=110000\ milligrams=110\ grams$$
The corresponding iron amount is 85–110 grams. It is not 85–110 grams of ferrous sulphate or ferrous fumarate: carrier mass depends on iron fraction, chemical form and purity.
Calculation 2 — Oil vitamin units
The schedule states:
$$1\ international\ unit\ of\ vitamin\ A=0.3\ microgram\ retinol\ equivalent$$
Thus:
$$6\div0.3=20\ international\ units\ per\ gram$$
$$9.9\div0.3=33\ international\ units\ per\ gram$$
Oil vitamin A range: 20–33 international units per gram.
For vitamin D:
$$1\ international\ unit=0.025\ microgram$$
$$0.11\div0.025=4.4\ international\ units\ per\ gram$$
$$0.16\div0.025=6.4\ international\ units\ per\ gram$$
Oil vitamin D range: 4.4–6.4 international units per gram. These conversions do not remove the plant-source requirement.
Calculation 3 — Milk vitamin units
Vitamin A:
$$270\div0.3=900\ international\ units\ per\ litre$$
$$450\div0.3=1500\ international\ units\ per\ litre$$
Vitamin D:
$$5\div0.025=200\ international\ units\ per\ litre$$
$$7.5\div0.025=300\ international\ units\ per\ litre$$
Milk ranges are therefore 900–1500 international units per litre for vitamin A and 200–300 international units per litre for vitamin D.
Calculation 4 — Negative label tolerance
Assume, solely for illustration, that the declared total value of a nutrient is 35 milligrams per kilogram and that the relevant added-nutrient declaration is within its applicable Schedule I range.
$$10\%\ of\ 35=0.10\times35=3.5\ milligrams\ per\ kilogram$$
$$35-3.5=31.5\ milligrams\ per\ kilogram$$
The numerical minus-ten-percent point is 31.5 milligrams per kilogram.

This calculation illustrates the stated tolerance only. It does not authorize a declaration outside the prescribed range, abolish the maximum added-nutrient limit, establish the treatment of every intrinsic-nutrient contribution, or create a universal Schedule III tolerance.
Calculation 5 — Twice-yearly quality assurance undertaking
$$1\ year\times2\ undertakings\ per\ year=2\ undertakings$$

“Twice a year” is the stated submission frequency. It does not mean that monitoring, inventory maintenance or testing occurs only twice a year. The listed controls include continuous inventory, stage-wise monitoring and regular audit.
